title: Why Almost Nobody Lives in Wyoming
sources: Railway band: own count from 2020 census block groups (US Census Bureau) (geo/measure_rail.py)
Federal land: BLM Surface Management Agency; counties: US Census Bureau; states and countries: Natural Earth (geo/make_regions.py)
Checkerboard squares at Elk Mountain: illustration of the 1862 grant pattern, not surveyed parcels
Trail, railway, train and route lines drawn through main points (approximate)

paragraphs.text: Half a million people crossed Wyoming on the way west. Almost none of them stayed.
Today Wyoming is bigger than the United Kingdom. But fewer people live in the whole state than in Washington, D.C.

shots.on_screen_text: The United Kingdom at the same scale

paragraphs.text: Its biggest town, Cheyenne, has about sixty-five thousand people. Drive west from it on the interstate, and the houses run out within minutes.

shots.on_screen_text: The old Union Pacific depot, Cheyenne

shots.photo: File:I-80 toward Rawlins and Laramie - Wyoming (53577131945).jpg

paragraphs.text: This is a state where cattle barons once hired gunmen to decide who could own a piece of it. Where four hunters were sued for millions because of a single step across a corner. And where a whole town of four thousand people emptied in a few years.
So why does almost nobody live in Wyoming? There are six reasons, and every one of them still shows on the map today. The first is the reason all those travellers kept walking.
Reason one. Wyoming was built as a way through, not a place to stop.

shots.photo: File:B-14. South Pass Overlook (west of South Pass City) on the California, Mormon Pioneer, and Oregon National Historic Trails (2003) (49008a89-8329-4aac-93d1-cd43c3407933).JPG

paragraphs.text: Between 1840 and 1869, about half a million emigrants crossed it on the Oregon, California and Mormon trails. Almost all of them used one gap in the Rocky Mountains: South Pass.

stat.label: Emigrants on the Oregon, California and Mormon trails, 1840-1869

shots.photo: File:Alfred Jacob Miller - Fort Laramie - Walters 37194049.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Fort Laramie, painted by Alfred Jacob Miller, 1850s

shots.photo: File:South Pass Area of Critical Environmental Concern, Wyoming (15472769319).jpg

paragraphs.text: South Pass is so wide and gentle that wagons could roll over the Continental Divide without a road. It is also more than seven thousand feet above the sea.

shots.photo: File:This broad open saddle called South Pass in Wyoming located on the continental divide is one of the high points along the Oregon (f87089a1-155d-451f-67c6-1277b1f30ec3).JPG
shots.on_screen_text: South Pass, on the Continental Divide

stat.label: South Pass, the emigrants' crossing

paragraphs.text: The travellers stopped only where they had to. Fort Laramie, on the North Platte, was a trading post and later an army fort where wagons rested and mended. Fort Bridger, in the far southwest, sold supplies to the people heading for Utah and California. These were service stations, not towns.

shots.on_screen_text: Fort Laramie and the North Platte

shots.photo: File:Fort Laramie. Post as it appeared in 1868. Orginally located as a fur trading post in 1834, known as Fort William... - NARA - 516878.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Fort Laramie as it was in 1868
Register Cliff, where emigrants carved their names

paragraphs.text: So many wagons used the same track near today's town of Guernsey that their wheels cut grooves into the sandstone, in places five feet deep. You can still walk in them.

shots.on_screen_text: The Oregon Trail ruts at Guernsey

shots.photo: File:A-12. The Bedlam Ruts (west of Fort Laramie National Historic Site) on the California, Mormon Pioneer, and Oregon National Historic Trails (2006) (a3b55225-3e5d-4675-8d62-e97ef09219a1).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Wagon ruts west of Fort Laramie

paragraphs.text: And that is Wyoming's first problem. The average height of the whole state is about six thousand seven hundred feet. Only Colorado sits higher.

stat.label: Wyoming's average elevation

paragraphs.text: Up there, summer is short. In the high basins, frost can come in any month. On average the state gets about thirteen inches of rain and snow a year. In the western basins it is under ten. Iowa's farms get more than twice as much.

shots.photo: File:Greater Sage-Grouse in Red Desert, WY (7487155676).jpg
File:Artemesia tridentata var wyomingensis Wyoming big sagebrush (52752054243).jpg

stat.label: Rain and snow a year, Wyoming average (1961-1990)
stat.source: National Atlas of the United States

paragraphs.text: In the middle of the state lies the Great Divide Basin, where the Continental Divide splits in two. Rain that falls here never reaches any ocean. It sinks into the ground or dries up where it lands.

shots.photo: File:Bikepacking through Great Divide Basin, Wyoming, USA.jpg

paragraphs.text: And then there is the wind. Southern Wyoming is one of the windiest places in the lower forty-eight states. On Interstate 80, gusts of sixty miles an hour close the road to light, high-sided trucks. Even so, the wind blows over about forty-seven vehicles a year on that one highway.

shots.photo: File:I-80 toward Rawlins and Laramie - Wyoming (53577131945).jpg

stat.label: Gusts that close I-80 to light, high-profile vehicles
Vehicles blown over on I-80 (five-year average)

paragraphs.text: For a family with an ox team and a plough, none of this looked like home. Oregon had rain. California had gold. Utah had a church waiting. Wyoming was the hard part in between.

shots.on_screen_text: A replica wagon on the emigrant trail

paragraphs.text: So for thirty years, people walked through. What finally made some of them stop was not the land. It was a railway.

shots.photo: File:Captain Andrew Joseph Russell - General John S. Casement and His Outfit - Google Art Project.jpg

paragraphs.text: Reason two. Wyoming's towns were not settled. They were placed, one by one, along a railway line.

In July 1867, there was nothing at the spot the railway surveyors picked beside Crow Creek. In November the tracks arrived. By then about four thousand people were living there in tents and shacks. They called it Cheyenne, the Magic City of the Plains.

shots.photo: File:Granite cut, near Dale Creek bridge, West Cheyenne. Albany County, Wyoming. - NARA - 516612.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Union Pacific cut west of Cheyenne, about 1869

stat.label: People in Cheyenne when the tracks arrived, November 1867

shots.photo: File:"Cheyenne, Wyo., 1876." General view of this town on the Oregon Trail - NARA - 531115.tif

paragraphs.text: Then the line moved on, and new towns sprang up along it every few dozen miles. Laramie. Rawlins. Rock Springs. Green River. Evanston.

shots.on_screen_text: Citadel Rock and the new line near Green River, 1868

paragraphs.text: Some of those towns did not survive the summer. Benton, in the desert east of Rawlins, was the end of the track in 1868. For a few weeks it had about three thousand people, saloons and gambling halls. Then the tracks moved west, the people followed, and within about three months Benton was gone. Today there is nothing on the spot but sagebrush.

stat.label: People in Benton, summer 1868

shots.on_screen_text: Near the Benton site, by today's Sinclair

paragraphs.text: Towns like this were called Hell on Wheels. They were not settlements. They were the railway's camp, packed up and carried west on flatcars.

shots.photo: File:Dale Creek Bridge Union Pacific Railroad Company by Andrew J Russell.jpg
File:Generals Grant, Sherman, Sheridan, Hooker, Harney, Dodge, Gibbon, and Potter at Fort Sanders LCCN2013647598.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Grant, Sherman and the railway's engineer Dodge at Fort Sanders, 1868

paragraphs.text: We measured where Wyoming's people live today, using every neighbourhood in the 2020 census. A band twelve miles either side of the old line covers a tenth of the state. More than a third of all Wyomingites live inside it. Most of the rest live in towns that later booms built, like Casper and Gillette.

chart.title: Within 20 km of the 1868 line
chart.source: Own count: 2020 census block groups vs the 1868 line (geo/measure_rail.py)

paragraphs.text: Look at the map with the railway hidden, and you can still draw it from the lights at night. A line of towns across the south, and in the north and the middle, darkness with a few bright spots, mostly mine and oil towns.

The railway left something else behind. To pay for it, Congress gave the Union Pacific every other square mile of land for twenty miles on each side of the track. The government kept the squares in between.

stat.label: Railroad grant on each side of the track: every other square mile

paragraphs.text: The result is a checkerboard, hundreds of miles long. Private square, public square, private square. They touch only at their corners.

stat.label: Public squares meet only at their corners

paragraphs.text: For a century and a half, that left a question nobody had settled. Can you step from one public square to the next, across the corner, without touching private land?

In 2021, four hunters from Missouri did exactly that on Elk Mountain, using a small ladder. The ranch belonged to a North Carolina businessman. His company sued them, claiming the step had cost the ranch up to seven point seven five million dollars in value.

stat.label: Four Missouri hunters cross a corner at Elk Mountain

shots.photo: File:BLM Wyoming- Salt Wells Creek Herd Management Area (19834956313).jpg

stat.label: Damage the ranch's company claimed

paragraphs.text: The hunters won in court in 2023, and again on appeal in 2025. In October 2025 the Supreme Court declined to hear the case. Across the West, about eight million acres of public land are locked in corners like these.

stat.label: District court, then the 10th Circuit, rule for the hunters
The Supreme Court declines the case (No. 25-64)
Public land locked behind corners in the West

paragraphs.text: Before that, the hunters had also been charged with criminal trespass in Carbon County. In April 2022 a local jury found them not guilty, after deliberating for less than two hours.

stat.label: Carbon County jury, 29 April 2022, after under two hours

paragraphs.text: A railway decided where Wyoming's towns would be. But who would own the land between them was decided by something else. Cattle, and the men who owned them.

shots.photo: File:"Cheyenne, Wyo., 1876." General view of this town on the Oregon Trail - NARA - 531115.tif

paragraphs.text: Reason three. Wyoming's open land was claimed early by a few very large cattle companies, and they fought to keep it that way.

shots.on_screen_text: Cattle on the open range, Pinedale

paragraphs.text: In the 1870s and early 1880s, the grass between the railway and the mountains was open range. Anyone could graze it. Investors in Britain and in the eastern states poured money into cattle companies. In Cheyenne, their managers built a club with a wine cellar and a chef.

By late 1886 there were close to nine hundred thousand cattle in Wyoming, far more than the grass could carry. Then came the winter of 1886 and 1887. Storm after storm buried the range. Many herds were never found again until the spring melt.

stat.label: Cattle in Wyoming, late 1886

shots.photo: File:Artemesia tridentata var wyomingensis Wyoming big sagebrush (52752054243).jpg

stat.label: The winter that ended the open range

paragraphs.text: The big companies came out of that winter weaker and angrier. Small ranchers and homesteaders were moving onto the land they had treated as theirs. The big outfits called many of them rustlers, cattle thieves.

shots.photo: File:Looking northwest past Ranch House and Barn toward Grand Teton - T. A. Moulton Ranch, Mormon Row Road, Kelly, Teton County, WY HABS WYO,20-KEL.V,2-9.tif

stat.label: What the big outfits called many small ranchers

paragraphs.text: In April 1892, the Wyoming Stock Growers Association acted. A special train left Cheyenne carrying about fifty armed men, among them two dozen gunmen hired in Texas. They carried a list of names.

shots.on_screen_text: Cheyenne, where the special train left

stat.label: Armed men on the train, two dozen hired in Texas

paragraphs.text: On the ninth of April they surrounded a cabin at the KC Ranch. Inside was Nate Champion, a small rancher who had stood up to the big outfits. He held them off all day. Between the shots, he wrote in a pocket diary. His last line was signed: "Nathan D. Champion." That evening they set the cabin on fire and shot him as he ran.

shots.on_screen_text: Kaycee, by the old KC Ranch

stat.label: Nate Champion besieged at the KC Ranch
How his diary ends, 9 April 1892

shots.on_screen_text: The Powder River country near Kaycee

paragraphs.text: The delay cost them. Word reached Buffalo, the county seat, and a posse of several hundred local men rode out. They trapped the invaders at the TA Ranch and laid siege for two days.

shots.on_screen_text: The TA Ranch, on Crazy Woman Creek

paragraphs.text: Then a telegram reached the White House. President Benjamin Harrison sent the cavalry from Fort McKinney. The invaders surrendered to the soldiers, not to the sheriff. None of them was ever convicted.

stat.label: President Harrison orders the cavalry in
None of the invaders was ever convicted

paragraphs.text: Wyoming had become a state less than two years before. The census of 1890 had counted about sixty-two thousand people in it. In the place where Wyoming's open land was divided, the people with the most land were also the people with the most power.

stat.label: People in Wyoming, 1890 census

paragraphs.text: The territory had already tried an unusual way to attract settlers. In December 1869, Wyoming became the first place in the United States where women could vote and hold office. Men far outnumbered women in the territory. Some lawmakers backed the vote on principle. Others hoped it would bring families west. It made Wyoming the Equality State. It did not make it crowded.

shots.photo: File:Woman suffrage in Wyoming Territory. - Scene at the polls in Cheyenne - from a photo. by Kirkland. LCCN92516129.jpg#crop=0.12,0.22,0.12,0.06
shots.on_screen_text: Women at the polls in Cheyenne, 1888

stat.label: Women's vote in Wyoming Territory, the first in the US

shots.photo: File:Generals Grant, Sherman, Sheridan, Hooker, Harney, Dodge, Gibbon, and Potter at Fort Sanders LCCN2013647598.jpg

paragraphs.text: And there was a deeper reason the small homesteads struggled. A federal homestead was a hundred and sixty acres. In Iowa that was a farm. In Wyoming's dry grass, it could not feed a herd big enough to live on.

stat.label: A homestead under the 1862 Act

paragraphs.text: Much of the land the homesteaders never took stayed with the government. And that is where the story of Wyoming's emptiness gets bigger than any ranch.

shots.photo: File:BLM Wyoming- Salt Wells Creek Herd Management Area (19834956313).jpg

paragraphs.text: Hold on to that, because the last three reasons are the ones that still decide where people live in Wyoming today.
Reason four. Almost half of Wyoming still belongs to the federal government, and it is not for sale.

stat.label: Federal share of Wyoming's land (our own count: 47 %)

paragraphs.text: It started in 1872, when Congress set aside Yellowstone in the corner of the territory as the world's first national park.

Then came national forests in the mountains. And the leftover range that nobody had claimed became public grazing land, run since 1946 by the Bureau of Land Management. Today it holds more than eighteen million acres in Wyoming alone.

shots.photo: File:South Pass Area of Critical Environmental Concern, Wyoming (15472769319).jpg

stat.label: BLM land in Wyoming

shots.on_screen_text: BLM land in the Red Desert

paragraphs.text: The turning point came in 1934. The Taylor Grazing Act put the remaining open range under federal management, and within a year most of it was closed to new homestead claims. The last great chance to hand Wyoming's land to settlers, one family at a time, was over.

stat.label: Taylor Grazing Act

shots.photo: File:Greater Sage-Grouse in Red Desert, WY (7487155676).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Open range in the Red Desert

shots.photo: File:Looking northwest past Ranch House and Barn toward Grand Teton - T. A. Moulton Ranch, Mormon Row Road, Kelly, Teton County, WY HABS WYO,20-KEL.V,2-9.tif

paragraphs.text: Federal land is open to hikers, hunters and grazing. But you cannot build a town on it. Most of the land in Wyoming where a new suburb could go is simply not available.
Nowhere is that clearer than in Jackson Hole. More than nine-tenths of Teton County is national park, national forest or wildlife refuge. The private land is a sliver along the valley floor.

stat.label: Federal land in Teton County
stat.source: Own measurement: BLM Surface Management Agency data (geo/make_regions.py)

paragraphs.text: The view brought the wealthy, and the sliver became some of the most expensive land in America. By the government's own count, Teton County has the highest income per person of any county in the country. Many of the people who work there cannot afford to live there, and drive in over a mountain pass from Idaho.

shots.on_screen_text: The National Elk Refuge beside Jackson

stat.label: Income per person, of all US counties

paragraphs.text: So the land is high, dry and largely closed. But Wyoming is rich, not poor. Under that land lies some of the biggest energy wealth in America. And that is where the fifth reason begins, because the wealth itself kept emptying the towns.
Reason five. In Wyoming, minerals bring people in fast, and take them away just as fast.

The railway had found the first underground wealth. The Union Pacific needed coal for its locomotives, and it opened mines at Rock Springs, Hanna and Carbon. In the early 1950s the railway switched to diesel. It closed its Hanna mines in 1954 and its last Rock Springs mine in 1962, and the towns around them shrank.

shots.on_screen_text: The Union Pacific line at Green River, 1868

stat.label: Union Pacific trades steam for diesel, early 1950s
Union Pacific shuts its Hanna mines

paragraphs.text: Even the oil was decided far away. In 1922, the Secretary of the Interior quietly leased a naval oil reserve north of Casper, called Teapot Dome, to an oil tycoon who had sent him hundreds of thousands of dollars in bonds. Albert Fall became the first cabinet secretary in American history to go to prison.

shots.on_screen_text: Albert Fall, Secretary of the Interior

shots.photo: File:Harry F. Sinclair, multimillionaire oil magnate (left) and his counsel Martin W. Littleton. Teapot Dome hearing LCCN2016893277.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Harry Sinclair at the Teapot Dome hearings

shots.photo: File:Former Secretary of Interior found guilty of bribery. Albert B. Fall, former Secretary of Interior, leaving the District and Supreme Court in Washington today surrounded by members of his LCCN2016889499.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Albert Fall after the guilty verdict, 1929

paragraphs.text: Uranium told the same story in a smaller place. In 1957 a mill opened in central Wyoming, and Jeffrey City grew around it. By 1980 more than four thousand people lived there, with a school, a swimming pool and a bowling alley.

stat.label: People in Jeffrey City, 1980

paragraphs.text: But after the accident at Three Mile Island in 1979, the price of uranium fell. In the early 1980s the mines closed. By 1988 Jeffrey City was nearly empty. In 2010 the census counted fifty-eight people.

stat.label: Three Mile Island; uranium prices fall

shots.on_screen_text: Jeffrey City and the empty plain

stat.label: People in Jeffrey City, 2010 census

paragraphs.text: Coal made the biggest boom of all. In the Powder River Basin, the coal lies in seams so thick and so close to the surface that it is scraped up by machines the size of buildings.
Gillette grew so fast in the 1970s that a psychologist gave the problems a name: the Gillette Syndrome. Crime, drinking, broken marriages, and families living in trailers in the mud.

stat.label: "Gillette Syndrome": a psychologist names the boomtown's troubles

paragraphs.text: Wyoming's coal peaked in 2008, at more than four hundred and sixty million tons. By 2024 it had fallen to about one hundred and ninety million, the lowest since 1992. Power plants across America were switching to gas and wind.

And even at the top of the boom, coal never needed many people. The machines did the work. North Antelope Rochelle, the biggest coal mine in the country, dug about sixty-five million tons in 2025. It did it with around eleven hundred workers.

shots.photo: File:Coal Haul Truck at North Antelope Rochelle.png
shots.on_screen_text: A haul truck at North Antelope Rochelle

stat.label: North Antelope Rochelle, 2025
Workers at the mine

paragraphs.text: So the money stayed. Wyoming has no state income tax and billions saved in a mineral trust fund. But the jobs did not. And the people who notice that first are the young.

stat.label: Wyoming levies no state income tax

shots.on_screen_text: The Wyoming Union, University of Wyoming

paragraphs.text: Reason six. Wyoming raises its children well, and then loses most of them.
The state has one public four-year university, in Laramie, a town of about thirty thousand. There is no big city with offices, hospitals and companies where a graduate can build a career.

shots.photo: File:Arts and Sciences Building - University of Wyoming - Laramie (52040416492).jpg

paragraphs.text: A study by Harvard's Growth Lab in 2024 followed people born in Wyoming. By their thirties, nearly two in every three had left the state. That is one of the highest rates in the country.

stat.label: Harvard Growth Lab: Wyoming growth diagnostic
Born in Wyoming, gone by their thirties

paragraphs.text: Most of them did not go far. Fort Collins and Denver are an hour or two south. The same mountains, the same dry air, but a metro of about three million people, an airport with flights to the world, and jobs that do not depend on the price of coal.

stat.label: People in the Denver metro area

paragraphs.text: Colorado had the same Rockies and the same dry plains. But it found gold in 1858, became a state in 1876, and gained federal offices, universities and an airline hub that Wyoming never had. Colorado now has just over six million people, ten times Wyoming's population, on a state not much bigger.

stat.label: Gold found near today's Denver

paragraphs.text: That is the loop Wyoming is caught in. Few people means few employers. Few employers means the young leave. And when they leave, there are fewer people again.

So that is why almost nobody lives in Wyoming. The land is high and dry, so the travellers kept walking. The railway put the towns in a single line. The cattle kings fought to keep the range in a few hands. The government kept the rest. The minerals came and went in booms. And the young leave for Colorado.

shots.photo: File:This broad open saddle called South Pass in Wyoming located on the continental divide is one of the high points along the Oregon (f87089a1-155d-451f-67c6-1277b1f30ec3).JPG
File:Coal Haul Truck at North Antelope Rochelle.png
File:Arts and Sciences Building - University of Wyoming - Laramie (52040416492).jpg

paragraphs.text: The four hunters won their case, and the ruling now covers corners like theirs in six western states. The men who rode north from Cheyenne in 1892 were never punished, and the big ranches are still there. And Jeffrey City, the town of four thousand, is a street grid in the sagebrush with a few dozen people.

stat.label: The invaders were never punished

paragraphs.text: Now Wyoming is betting on something new. In Carbon County, on the same windy range the railway crossed, a wind farm of about six hundred turbines is being built. It will be the largest power plant in the state.

shots.on_screen_text: The Chokecherry and Sierra Madre site

stat.label: Chokecherry and Sierra Madre wind project

paragraphs.text: And in Kemmerer, a coal town in the southwest, construction began in 2026 on a new kind of nuclear plant, next to the coal plant it is meant to replace.

stat.label: TerraPower's reactor: construction permit 4 March 2026

paragraphs.text: Both bring money and, while they are built, thousands of workers. But once they run, the wind farm expects about a hundred and fourteen permanent jobs. The reactor, about two hundred and fifty. Wind and atoms will not fill Wyoming either.

shots.on_screen_text: The wind farm site, Carbon County

stat.label: Permanent jobs at the wind farm (developer's estimate)
Permanent jobs at the Natrium plant (estimate)

paragraphs.text: Maybe that is not a failure. Wyoming has fewer people than any other state, and many of the people who live there would like it to stay that way. Would you take that much space, if the nearest city were three hours away?

shots.photo: File:B-14. South Pass Overlook (west of South Pass City) on the California, Mormon Pioneer, and Oregon National Historic Trails (2003) (49008a89-8329-4aac-93d1-cd43c3407933).JPG
File:Bikepacking through Great Divide Basin, Wyoming, USA.jpg

ask.text: Would you take that much space, three hours from the nearest city?

youtube.description: Wyoming is bigger than the United Kingdom, yet fewer people live in the whole state than in Washington, D.C. Half a million emigrants crossed it on the way west and almost none stayed. We follow the answer on the map and in the archives: South Pass and the emigrant trails, the 1868 Union Pacific line that still holds a third of the people on a tenth of the land, the checkerboard and the corner-crossing hunters, the cattle kings and the Johnson County War, the federal land nobody can buy, Teapot Dome, Jeffrey City and the Powder River coal, and the young people who leave for Colorado.
